questions.q: The Hammett equation is:
c: log k = a + b log t
questions.e: σ describes the substituent, ρ the reaction's sensitivity.

questions.q: A positive ρ value indicates that the reaction is:
c: Accelerated by electron-withdrawing substituents, consistent with negative charge build-up in the TS
questions.e: Positive ρ: substituents with positive σ (EWG) increase rate.

questions.q: Which set of σ_para values is typical?
questions.e: Electron-withdrawing groups have positive σ, donors negative.

questions.q: A Hammett plot is V-shaped (or has a sharp break) across substituents. What does it suggest?
questions.m: A change in mechanism or in the rate-determining step as the substituent electronics change (for example from a rate-limiting step with negative charge build-up to one with positive charge build-up). A V-shaped plot indicates opposite signs of ρ for the two regimes. Curved plots can also reflect a change in rate-determining step in multi-step reactions.

questions.q: A primary deuterium kinetic isotope effect (k_H/k_D ≈ 2–7) implies that:
c: The C–H bond is broken in the rate-determining step
The C–H bond is not involved at all
questions.e: Zero-point energy differences make C–H cleavage faster than C–D cleavage.

questions.q: A small normal secondary KIE (k_H/k_D ≈ 1.1–1.25) at a carbon becoming sp² (e.g., SN1 ionization) reflects:
c: Loosening of out-of-plane C–H bending vibrations on rehybridization
questions.e: The bending modes become less restricted in the sp² cation, favoring the lighter isotope.

questions.q: The Curtin–Hammett principle states that when conformers interconvert rapidly relative to product formation:
c: The product ratio reflects the difference in free energies of the transition states, not the ground-state populations
The product ratio equals the ratio of conformer populations
The more stable conformer always gives the major product
questions.e: It lets you compare TS energies directly.

questions.q: Contrast the conditions that give kinetic versus thermodynamic enolates of an unsymmetrical ketone.
questions.m: Kinetic enolate (less substituted): strong, bulky, non-nucleophilic base (LDA), low temperature (−78 °C), aprotic solvent (THF), short time, irreversible deprotonation. Thermodynamic enolate (more substituted, more stable): weaker/protic conditions or excess ketone, higher temperature, longer times allowing equilibration (e.g., NaOEt/EtOH or NaH, room temp).

questions.q: The main stabilizing effect that makes tertiary carbocations more stable than primary is:
c: Hyperconjugation with adjacent C–H/C–C σ bonds
questions.e: σ-bond donation into the empty p orbital delocalizes charge.

questions.q: Acid treatment of a vicinal diol such as pinacol (2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol) gives:
questions.e: Ionization, a 1,2-methyl shift, and loss of H⁺ form 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanone.

questions.q: The 2-norbornyl cation was proposed to be non-classical because:
c: σ-Bond participation delocalizes charge over a bridged structure
It has a vacant d orbital
questions.e: Evidence includes rate and stereochemical data on exo/endo solvolysis.

questions.q: Why does exo-2-norbornyl brosylate solvolyze faster than the endo isomer and give racemic exo product?
questions.m: In the exo isomer the C1–C6 σ bond is anti-periplanar to the leaving group and can participate (anchimeric assistance), delivering a bridged, delocalized (non-classical) cation and accelerating ionization. The bridged symmetric cation is captured from the exo face by nucleophile, giving racemic exo product. The endo isomer lacks the anti-periplanar σ bond and ionizes more slowly.

questions.q: A thermal [4+2] cycloaddition is allowed when:
c: It proceeds suprafacially on both components
It is antarafacial on both components
questions.e: 6 electrons (4n+2) with all suprafacial components is thermally allowed.

questions.q: A thermal [2+2] cycloaddition between two simple alkenes, suprafacial on both, is:
Thermal electrocyclic ring closure of a conjugated diene (4π electrons) proceeds by:
Explain how FMO theory predicts the rate and regiochemistry of a normal electron-demand Diels–Alder reaction.
questions.m: The dominant interaction is HOMO(diene)–LUMO(dienophile). Electron-withdrawing groups on the dienophile lower its LUMO and decrease the energy gap, speeding the reaction. Regiochemistry follows the largest orbital coefficients: the termini with the largest HOMO and LUMO coefficients bond preferentially, giving the 'ortho' and 'para' products for 1-substituted and 2-substituted dienes with a monosubstituted dienophile.

questions.q: The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction couples:
c: An aryl halide with an organoboron compound, using Pd and a base
An aryl halide with an alkyne using Cu
questions.e: The base activates boron for transmetalation.

questions.q: The fundamental steps of a Pd(0)/Pd(II) cross-coupling cycle are:
questions.e: Heck couplings substitute migratory insertion/β-H elimination for transmetalation.

questions.q: Count the valence electrons for Pd(PPh₃)₄ and say what the 18-electron rule predicts.
questions.m: Pd(0) is d¹⁰ (10 electrons) plus four PPh₃ ligands donating 2 each (8) = 18 electrons, a saturated, stable complex. In solution it dissociates ligands to give the reactive 16- or 14-electron species Pd(PPh₃)₃/Pd(PPh₃)₂ that undergo oxidative addition.

questions.q: According to the Zimmerman–Traxler model, a Z-enolate generally gives which aldol diastereomer?
questions.e: A chair TS with the aldehyde substituent equatorial: Z → syn, E → anti.

questions.q: Evans oxazolidinone auxiliaries with Bu₂BOTf/amine base give which type of aldol selectivity?
c: syn aldol via a Z-boron enolate
anti aldol via an E-boron enolate
questions.e: The Z(O)-boron enolate reacts through a chair TS, and the auxiliary controls the face.
